Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most popular and fastest growing technologies over the past half decade because of its wide range of uses and applications. AI can be an extremely useful tool for many different jobs, however, as it has become more widespread it has been used to replace “Human Intelligence”. In my opinion, generally, generative AI use is acceptable when it is moderate and not used for entire projects and presented as one’s own individual work. Generative AI should only be used as a helping tool to either aid with learning or assist in specific problem solving cases.

title: AI Usage
text:
My AI Use
When it comes to my school/professional work I rarely use generative AI beyond basic queries. I mainly use Large Language Models (LLM) like ChatGPT as an advanced search engine, for when my questions may be too specific to get an instant answer from Google. For example, when working on a coding project, sometimes I get errors that I have not seen before or are not easily readable, in this case I paste the error message into an LLM to get a detailed description of the error message and the common causes for it.

title: Can Dogs Learn Words by Overhearing
text: In this assignment we explore the idea of dogs learning the names of objects by overhearing the object being referenced in outside conversation without being directly taught. Dror et al. (2026) conducted a study where 10 dogs were exposed to a condition where two family members sitting across from each other passing the toy back and forth. The caretaker addressed the second person using simple sentence frames and non-verbal cues, neither directly to the dog.

title: Can Dogs Learn Words by Overhearing
text:
Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test
I performed two two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test with a confidence level of \(95\%\) for the Overhearing data and Difference data. My hypotheses are below.
Overhearing Data: \[
H_0 : \text{median}(X) = 50\% \newline
H_a : \text{median}(X) \neq 50\%
\] Difference Data: \[
H_0 : \text{median}(X) = 0 \newline
H_a : \text{median}(X) \neq 0
\]

Test Results

The \(p\)-value for the Overhearing data is less than \(0.025\) so we have evidence to reject the null hypothesis, there is evidence that the dogs did not retrieve the correct toy by chance. The \(p\)-value for the Difference data is much greater than \(0.025\), however, so we do not reject the null hypothesis, there is not sufficient evidence that the dogs retrieve the toys more or less successfully when learning their names directly or from overhearing.





Wilcoxon Distribution with Rejection Region and Observed Values



This graph shows the Wilcoxon distribution for a sample of size \(n = 10\), along with the rejection region for a two-sided test (\(\alpha = 0.025\) on either side). We can see that the Wilcoxon score for the Difference data (\(W = 21.5\)) lies near the middle of the distribution so we do not reject the null in this case. However, the Wilcoxon score for the Overhearing data (\(W = 54.0\)) lies far in the rejection region so we do reject the null.
